UK TREASURY GUIDANCE

Four conditions separate a saving from an estimate.

27 / 29
  1. Already happenedThe cash relates to an activity that has taken place
  2. Not moved or deferredCosts are not merely relocated or deferred
  3. Net of double countingNo benefit is claimed twice
  4. Reasonable to a third partyAn impartial reviewer would accept it

Deadweight Outcomes that would have occurred without any intervention are not a benefit.

Everything so far leads to a test you can apply without any technical knowledge. The British government's definition of a cashable saving sets six conditions. Four matter most here. The cash must relate to an activity that has already happened. Costs must not merely be relocated or deferred. The saving must be net of any double counting. And it must be reasonable to an impartial third party.

Add one more test from the Treasury's Green Book, on additionality. Deadweight describes outcomes that would have occurred without any intervention. A benefit the market would have delivered anyway is not a benefit of your project. Anything that fails these tests is an estimate. The surveys suggest an estimate is what most organisations hold.
